questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Structure of an argument
questions.learningObjective: Identify the main claim in an argument.

options.text: The main claim is the statement the whole argument defends.
The main claim is whichever sentence appears first in the text.
options.misconception: confuses sentence position with argumentative role

options.text: The main claim is any sentence that has evidence attached.
options.misconception: treats evidence presence as the claim itself

options.text: The main claim is the sentence with the strongest wording.

questions.explanation: The claim is the statement the argument supports; position, evidence, and wording do not define it.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Bias and the evidence for it
questions.learningObjective: Recognize bias in evidence.
questions.stem: Ticket 1002 notes that a reviewer always praises one framework; what bias does this show?

answer.exemplar: A strong answer identifies the bias, explains how it skews the reading of evidence, and suggests a fairer check for the reviewer.

questions.explanation: Bias skews interpretation; it does not make evidence false, vanish with size, or require dishonesty.
questions.hint: Ask how the evidence is read.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A claim the evidence does not support
questions.learningObjective: Spot a claim beyond the evidence.

stimulus.body: Ticket 1003 says the new cache cut latency by forty percent. It also says the team shipped three other changes the same week. No controlled comparison is described.

questions.stem: Ticket 1003 claims a rewrite will fix all bugs because the old code is messy.

options.text: A claim is unsupported only when no evidence exists.
options.misconception: requires zero evidence before calling a claim unsupported

options.text: A claim is unsupported when the evidence does not reach it.
A claim is supported if it sounds plausible.
options.misconception: confuses plausibility with evidential support

options.text: A claim is supported whenever it repeats the data.
options.misconception: treats repetition of data as proof

questions.explanation: Support depends on whether evidence reaches the claim; plausibility and repetition are not enough.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Inference that follows and one that does not
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish valid from invalid inference.
questions.stem: Ticket 1004 states two logs; what can be inferred and what cannot?

options.text: Any plausible guess counts as a valid inference.

options.text: An inference is valid if it matches prior belief.
